name: Self-fulfilling prophecy
statement: A false belief about a situation can make itself true, because people act on the belief and their actions produce the outcome it described.
meaning: The claim is causal and it starts from an error. A belief about how things stand is wrong, people act as though it were right, and their actions bring about the state of affairs the belief described. Falsity at the outset is the test, and it is what separates the idea from ordinary accurate prediction. The mechanism is behaviour rather than thought. Nothing in the account requires the believer to notice what they are doing, and in the laboratory versions the person who confirms the expectation does not know it exists. Two neighbouring subjects sit outside this entry. Teacher expectations and pupil IQ belong to the Pygmalion effect. Changed behaviour under observation belongs to the Hawthorne effect.

origin.where: The Antioch Review, volume 8, issue 2, pages 193-210
origin.note: Merton opens by crediting W. I. Thomas with the theorem 'If men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences', and says the same thought had been set out by Bossuet, Mandeville, Marx, Freud and Sumner before him. His illustration is fiction. In 1932 a solvent bank called the Last National fails after its depositors queue on a Black Wednesday. He then applies the pattern to the exclusion of black workers from American trade unions.

evidence: Merton ran no experiment. Two sets of figures in the paper come from outside the parable. Bank suspensions in the United States averaged 635 a year through the 1920s and 2,276 a year in the four years around the Crash, then fell to 28 a year in the twelve years after the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation was set up. In a biracial housing project in Pittsburgh, one white resident in 25 had expected relations between the races to run smoothly, and three of every four of the most apprehensive later reported that the races got along fairly well. The laboratory version arrived thirty years later. Snyder, Tanke and Berscheid paired 51 male with 51 female undergraduates at Minnesota and gave each man a Polaroid photograph of the woman he was about to telephone. The photographs were prepared in advance and assigned to pairs at random, so they carried no information about the woman on the line. Each pair talked for ten minutes, with the two voices recorded on separate channels. Twelve judges heard only the women's channel and knew nothing of the photographs. Women whose partners had been shown an attractive photograph came to behave in a friendly, likeable and sociable manner. Eden and Shani applied the same logic to 105 male Israeli military trainees, matched on aptitude and assigned at random to high, regular and unspecified instructor-expectancy conditions. The economic case is a model rather than a measurement. Diamond and Dybvig show that a demand deposit contract has more than one equilibrium, one of which is a run, and that anything which causes depositors to anticipate a run will produce one, including a bad earnings report, a run somewhere else, or sunspots.

replication.headline: The effect reproduces. Its size does not: estimates run from a correlation of about .2 across experiments to 73 percent of the variance in one military course.
replication.detail: Madon and colleagues ran four experiments on whether the effect adds up across perceivers. In three of them, with samples of 123 to 241, targets confirmed stereotypes about weight and sex more strongly when two perceivers held the expectation than when one did. They put the average self-fulfilling effect of a single perceiver at d = 0.65, close to the d = 0.60 they quote from Rosenthal for dyads. The second perceiver added d = 1.04 on top, for a combined d = 1.69. A fourth experiment, n = 121, found that fresh perceivers judged targets by the behaviour they had been channelled into, even when told that behaviour had been shaped by someone else. McNatt's meta-analysis of Pygmalion interventions among adults at work covered 17 studies, 58 effect sizes and 2,874 people, and reported an average of d = 1.13, stronger in the military, with men, and where expectations had been low to begin with. Jussim and colleagues put the same literature much lower. Averaging the meta-analyses of expectancy-confirming judgement gives r = .10, with individual entries running from 0 to .25, and they note that the meta-analyses with more studies gave systematically smaller effects, r = -.43 between effect size and study count. For self-fulfilment proper they give about .2 across experiments, ranging from 0 to about .3 outside military settings. Their central claim is about what the rest of the correlation is made of. Across naturalistic studies where both could be separated, accuracy accounted for roughly 75 percent of the link between expectation and outcome and self-fulfilment for about 25 percent. Jussim's later summary states that classic expectancy studies include multiple failed replications, and that expectations relate to social reality mainly because they reflect it rather than cause it. Guéguen and colleagues repeated the Snyder design online, with men answering personal advertisements carrying attractive or unattractive photographs. Replies to the attractive advertisements were longer and contained fewer spelling and grammatical errors.

study.cite: Madon, S., Jussim, L., Guyll, M., Nofziger, H., Salib, E. R., Willard, J., & Scherr, K. C. (2018). The accumulation of stereotype-based self-fulfilling prophecies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 115(5), 825-844.

replicated.weighting: average self-fulfilling effect of a single perceiver's stereotypic expectation across the three accumulation experiments, as reported by the authors

limits: Merton supplied no test. The bank is fictional, the bank-suspension counts are not a comparison of anything, and the housing survey is one project. No effect size is quoted here for Snyder, Tanke and Berscheid. Unpaywall records the article as closed with no repository copy, the publisher and PsycNET serve only the record, and no readable copy turned up in a web search. The design above was read off a conference paper Snyder gave on the same experiment in July 1977, deposited with ERIC, which reports the procedure and the direction of the result and no statistics. The Eden and Shani figure of 73 percent of variance was read from the abstract carried on Tel Aviv University's research record rather than from the article, and it rests on one course of 105 men. Jussim treats military settings as the place where these effects are largest, which is a reason to discount that number rather than to lead with it. Kierein and Gold's meta-analysis of Pygmalion effects in work organisations is a second workplace estimate. Wiley returned 403, and Crossref and Semantic Scholar both carry the record with the abstract withheld, so no figure from it appears on this page. The 75 percent accuracy share comes from five naturalistic studies of teachers, so it is a claim about classrooms generalised outwards. Averages across these meta-analyses pool manipulations that have little in common: a photograph, a briefing given to an instructor, a stereotype about body weight.
misreadings: The phrase has drifted to cover any prediction that comes true. Merton's requires the opening definition to be false, and where the expectation was right in the first place there is nothing to explain. That distinction is the whole of Jussim's case: expectations track outcomes largely because people judge each other reasonably well. The second misreading is optimistic. Merton's examples are a bank destroyed, a war brought on by the belief that it was coming, and a union that kept black workers out and then cited their strikebreaking as grounds. His remedy is institutional as well, deposit insurance rather than positive thinking, and he writes that the prophecy 'operates only in the absence of deliberate institutional controls'. A third is to treat the dyad as the ceiling. Madon and colleagues found the effect of one perceiver roughly doubled by a second, which is the mechanism by which small effects could matter and which they report as the first empirical support for a long-standing hypothesis. The Thomas theorem is not Merton's, and Merton says so in his first paragraph. The 2009 online replication of the attractiveness study names it after 'Snyder, Decker, and Bersheid' in its own title, dropping Elizabeth Decker Tanke's surname and misspelling Berscheid's.
